posts.text:
I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

It's deployed here: https://t.co/QMhmafXMj5 and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer:
posts.text_zh:
我让 Claude 用美国的真实数据去填充一张 Civilization 风格的游戏地图。Opus 5.5 下载并解析了大量公开数据，花了 7 小时、写了 45K 行代码之后……它能跑了 :)

- 31 个真实数据源，包括 Census、BEA、BLS、EIA、NOAA、USGS、DoD、NPS、FAA、FEMA、CDC……
- 真实的海拔、土地覆盖、GDP、就业、发电厂、矿场、港口、机场、军事基地、公园、大学、货运流、灾害；全部对齐到一张 25 km 的六边形网格上。
- 数据被转成了 Civilization 的语言，例如 Gold yield 就是 GDP。一座城市的 districts 是它真实的产业特长：San Jose 会有一座 Campus，Detroit 则是 "Motor city"。它的市民就是真实的劳动力构成：San Jose 每 4 个工作者里就有 1 个是工程师、程序员或科学家，全国平均是每 14 人里才有 1 个。Wonders 按已公布的规则选定，比如国家公园按游客量、大学按 R&D 支出，诸如此类。
- 19 种 lenses（收入、学历、信仰、灾害……），524 个都市区的 City View，以及九位顾问外加一个 Explorer。Explorer 可以把 3,100+ 个县的任意一列数据变成表格和散点图，并与地图联动。
- Claude 决定跳过了若干州和领地，抱歉
- 用 Claude Code 桌面应用构建，Opus 5.5 设为 medium，并打开了 ultracode。

部署在这里：https://t.co/QMhmafXMj5 ，"?" 里也有源码链接。我其实不太确定自己到底想做成什么样，但浏览和把玩起来真的很有意思。也许它可以继续扩展，或者做成一款游戏。不过我每周的 Claude 配额只剩一半了，所以得请别人接手了 :D。Claude 还做了支预告片：
配视频：30 秒 trailer，1920×1080。

quoted.text:
This is how I went from €0 MRR to building a SaaS that pays my bills.

A lot of people asked what happened in early 2025 that finally made this graph move.

So here's the story.

It actually started with a random video on X.

At the time, I was working a full time sales job after going back to employment from being self employed.

I had never heard of build in public and never seriously considered building a SaaS myself.

I knew how to code a little PHP, which I had taught myself back in 2020. But that was about it.

Then one day, @marclou's ShipFast launch video showed up on my timeline.

It was a Navy CIS style parody, and I thought it was hilarious.

I started following Marc, watched his livestreams, and eventually bought ShipFast.

His content was packed with practical advice, and watching him build products live helped me understand how this whole SaaS thing worked.

Remember, this was before AI coding tools became what they are today.

I was literally copying code into ChatGPT whenever I got stuck. (Instead of searching on Stack Overflow)

And I had never touched Next JS before.

But I wanted to learn.

So I started building.

My first project was a little website about children's books that I made with my girlfriend, who worked in childcare.

Nothing commercial. Just something to practice with.

Then I started building a vitamin.

I got pretty far before realizing I had absolutely no interest in the topic.

So I abandoned it.

Next, I tried building a SEO keyword research tool.

SEO tools were getting a lot of attention at the time, and I had some experience with SEO from my previous self-employment.

But while building it, I realized something.

I knew the basics of SEO, but nowhere near enough to build a genuinely good product in that space.

I would have needed to spend months learning the industry before even knowing what to build.

That's when I finally asked myself what I actually knew better than most people.

And the answer was obvious.

Affiliate marketing.

I'd been working in affiliate marketing since around 2011.

Over a decade of experience, recruiting affiliates, managing programs, working with different brands.

For the first time, I had an idea where my existing knowledge could actually give me an unfair advantage.

So I started researching the affiliate software market.

I noticed that SaaS founders were mostly using the same handful of platforms.

And I thought I could build something that made getting started with affiliate marketing easier and more affordable.

That's how Affonso started.

Around August or September 2024, I started building the first version.

The hardest part was Stripe.

I had never worked with Stripe before, and building reliable tracking for subscriptions, payments, and all the different edge cases took countless evenings.

The other nightmare was the landing page.

I'm terrible at design, but somehow still have pretty high standards. Not the greatest combination when you're building everything yourself. 😂

After roughly two months of working on it alongside my full-time job, I finally had something I could launch.

And it was VERY basic.

You could connect Stripe, create an affiliate program, generate tracking links, and see some basic analytics.

The affiliate portal was basically a link and a tiny chart.

There wasn't even a payout system yet.

And that was intentional.

One thing Marc kept repeating was to launch with the bare minimum.

I knew that even if someone signed up immediately, it would take time before their affiliates generated sales and commissions became payable.

So I decided to build payouts when someone actually needed them.

Which is exactly what I did.

I launched without a paywall. Anyone could sign up and use Affonso for free.

And then absolutely nothing happened.

I had a few users, but nobody was paying.

For weeks, I kept improving the product while trying to find people who might actually need it.

I had no testimonials, no reputation in the SaaS space, and no real audience.

And I refused to put fake testimonials on the landing page.

So I did the only thing I could think of.

I started talking to people.

I used X Pro to monitor conversations about affiliate software and SaaS affiliate programs.

Whenever someone had a question I could help with, I joined the conversation.

I wasn't pitching Affonso. I was trying to be useful.

And when someone showed genuine interest or mentioned a problem I knew I could solve, I'd reach out.

Sometimes we'd chat for a while before I even mentioned that I was building affiliate software.

Then I'd offer them free access and ask for feedback.

It was completely manual.

No automation, no AI outreach, no fancy growth strategy.

Just finding people with a relevant problem and talking to them.

But even with all that effort, getting the first paying customer took months.

By January 2025, I was seriously considering giving up.

I had already set myself a deadline. If nobody was willing to pay by then, I'd move on.

Around that time, I introduced something called the Revenue Pass.

Instead of offering a lifetime deal, I wanted to create an offer that was almost impossible to say no to.

For just $49, you could use Affonso until your affiliates had generated $10,000 in revenue.

The Revenue Pass gave customers a huge potential return for a tiny upfront investment while keeping the model sustainable.

And then it happened.

My first paying customer.

I actually reached out to him afterward.

He told me he loved the offer and wanted to secure it, even though he wasn't ready to actively work on affiliate marketing yet.

That one purchase meant so much to me.

After months of building and wondering whether anyone would ever pay, someone finally had.

And it gave me a reason to keep going.

About a week later, another purchase came in.

Then another.

At some point, I was getting two sales a week, then three, then four.

Eventually, people were buying Revenue Passes almost every day.

I gradually increased the price and eventually stopped selling them.

Meanwhile, more customers started choosing the regular subscription, which started at just $9/month.

And slowly, word of mouth started doing its thing too.

People were recommending Affonso to other founders.

The same people I had spent hours helping were now helping me grow.

Looking back at this chart, I think the biggest lesson is how unexciting the beginning actually was.

There was no big launch that changed everything.

I didn't have a huge following.
I didn't spend money on ads.
I didn't rank on Google.

I spent my evenings building a very basic product and my free time talking to potential customers.

And I kept doing that until something finally worked.

Today, Affonso pays my bills, supports my family, and allows me to work on something I genuinely enjoy full-time.

And it all started because a random video appeared on my timeline.

Funny how things work out.

If you're currently sitting at €0 MRR, don't underestimate how far you can get by simply talking to people and solving a problem you actually understand.
quoted.text_zh:
这就是我如何从 €0 MRR，做到做出一款能养活自己的 SaaS。

很多人问，2025 年初到底发生了什么，才终于让这张图开始往上走。

所以下面就是这个故事。

它其实始于 X 上一段随机刷到的视频。

那时，我刚从自雇重新回到全职工作，正在做一份全职销售。

我从未听说过 build in public，也从未认真考虑过自己去做一款 SaaS。

我会一点点 PHP，是 2020 年自学的。但仅此而已。

然后有一天，@marclou 的 ShipFast 上线视频出现在我的时间线上。

那是一个 Navy CIS 风格的恶搞，我觉得非常好笑。

我开始关注 Marc，看他的直播，最后买了 ShipFast。

他的内容里全是实用建议，看着他现场做产品，也帮我搞懂了 SaaS 这一整套是怎么运转的。

别忘了，那时候 AI 编程工具还远没有今天这个样子。

我一卡住，就是把代码复制进 ChatGPT。（而不是去 Stack Overflow 上搜）

而且我以前从未碰过 Next JS。

但我想学。

于是我开始动手做。

我的第一个项目，是和在托儿行业工作的女朋友一起做的一个关于童书的小网站。

不是商业项目，只是用来练习。

然后我开始做一个维生素相关的项目。

做了挺久，才意识到自己对这个话题完全没有兴趣。

于是放弃了。

接下来，我试着做一款 SEO 关键词研究工具。

当时 SEO 工具很受关注，而且我在之前自雇时也有一些 SEO 经验。

但做着做着，我意识到一件事。

我只懂 SEO 的皮毛，远不够在这个领域做出真正出色的产品。

我得先花几个月了解这个行业，才知道该做什么。

就在那时，我终于问自己：到底有什么是我比大多数人更懂的？

答案显而易见。

Affiliate marketing（联盟营销）。

我大概从 2011 年就开始做联盟营销了。

十多年的经验：招募 affiliates、管理项目、和不同品牌合作。

第一次，我有了一个能真正把已有知识变成不公平优势的想法。

于是我开始研究联盟软件市场。

我注意到，SaaS 创始人大多在用同一小撮平台。

我觉得自己可以做一个让联盟营销起步更简单、也更便宜的产品。

Affonso 就是这样开始的。

大概在 2024 年 8 月或 9 月，我开始做第一版。

最难的部分是 Stripe。

我以前从未用过 Stripe，要为订阅、支付以及各种边界情况做出可靠的追踪，花了无数个晚上。

另一场噩梦是落地页。

我设计很差，但不知怎么标准又挺高。什么都自己做的时候，这可不是什么好组合。😂

大概花了两个月，一边做全职工作一边开发，我终于有了可以上线的东西。

而且它非常非常基础。

你可以连接 Stripe、创建联盟项目、生成追踪链接，再看一些基础分析。

affiliate portal 基本上就是一个链接加一张很小的图表。

甚至还没有 payout（结算）系统。

而这是故意的。

Marc 反复强调的一点，就是用最低限度的功能先上线。

我知道，哪怕有人立刻注册，也得过一段时间，他们的 affiliates 才会带来销售，佣金才会真正需要支付。

所以我决定，等真有人需要结算时再去做 payouts。

我也正是这么做的。

我上线时没有付费墙。任何人都可以注册，免费使用 Affonso。

然后，什么都没发生。

有几个用户，但没有人付钱。

连续几周，我一边改进产品，一边试图找到真正可能需要它的人。

我没有推荐语，在 SaaS 圈子里没有声誉，也没有真正的受众。

而且我拒绝在落地页上放假推荐。

于是我做了当时唯一能想到的事。

我开始和人聊天。

我用 X Pro 监测关于联盟软件和 SaaS 联盟项目的讨论。

只要有人提出我能帮忙的问题，我就加入对话。

我不是在推销 Affonso，而是尽量变得有用。

当有人表现出真正的兴趣，或提到一个我知道自己能解决的问题时，我就会主动联系。

有时我们会先聊上一阵，我才提起自己正在做联盟软件。

然后我会给他们免费使用，并请他们给反馈。

这完全是手工的。

没有自动化，没有 AI 外联，也没有花哨的增长策略。

就是找到有相关问题的人，然后和他们聊。

但即便付出了这么多，等到第一个付费客户，还是花了好几个月。

到 2025 年 1 月，我已经在认真考虑放弃了。

我给自己设过一个截止日期：如果到那时还没人愿意付钱，我就换方向。

差不多在那个时候，我推出了一个叫 Revenue Pass 的东西。

我不想做 lifetime deal，而是想做一个几乎让人没法拒绝的报价。

只需 $49，你就可以一直用 Affonso，直到你的 affiliates 带来 $10,000 的收入。

Revenue Pass 用极低的预付成本给了客户巨大的潜在回报，同时又让模式本身可持续。

然后，它发生了。

我的第一位付费客户。

我后来还主动联系了他。

他告诉我，他很喜欢这个报价，想先把它锁定，尽管当时还没准备好真正去做联盟营销。

这一笔购买对我意义重大。

做了好几个月、一直怀疑会不会有人付钱之后，终于有人付了。

这也给了我继续做下去的理由。

大约一周后，又来了一笔。

然后又是一笔。

后来变成一周两单，再变成三单、四单。

最终，几乎每天都有人在买 Revenue Pass。

我逐渐提高了价格，最后停止了销售。

与此同时，越来越多客户开始选择普通订阅，起步价只有 $9/month。

慢慢地，口碑也开始发挥作用。

人们把 Affonso 推荐给其他创始人。

那些我曾花几个小时帮助过的人，现在反过来在帮我增长。

回看这张图，我觉得最大的教训是：开始阶段其实有多么平淡无奇。

并没有一次改变一切的大爆发上线。

我没有庞大的关注者。
我没有砸钱投广告。
我也没有在 Google 上排到前面。

我用晚上的时间做一个非常基础的产品，再用空闲时间跟潜在客户聊天。

然后一直这样做，直到终于有了效果。

如今，Affonso 能支付我的账单、养活我的家人，也让我能全职做一件自己真正喜欢的事。

而这一切，只是因为时间线上出现了一段随机视频。

事情就是这么奇妙。

如果你现在还停在 €0 MRR，不要低估一件事：只要愿意和人交流，并去解决一个你真正懂的问题，你能走得有多远。
